title: The best type is invisible.
metaDesc: Typography choices we make so you do not have to notice them.

texts.text: Typography choices we make so you do not have to notice them.

If someone reads your website and remembers the fonts you used, you failed. Typography should carry the voice of a brand without ever asking to be looked at. Here is how we think about type on every Mira project, and why restraint at this layer lets us be louder everywhere else on the page.

Every Mira project starts with the same type decision: one workhorse for body copy that reads for hours without effort, and one display face with enough personality to hold a headline. That is the whole system. No third face for accents. No decorative flourishes borrowed from moodboards. No condensed variant just because it looked good on Pinterest.

That is the whole system. No third face for accents. No decorative flourishes borrowed from moodboards. No condensed variant just because it looked good on Pinterest.

texts.text: Two faces is not a rule of taste. It is a rule of maintenance. Buyers of design templates and clients handing off brand systems always drift toward complexity. Every extra face is one more thing to police, one more chance for the system to break the moment a junior designer picks a heading style.

texts.text: When type stays quiet, everything around it gets to be loud. Bigger images. Bolder statements. More confident whitespace. This is the trade we make on every project. The typography is doing the invisible work of holding voice, so the rest of the design can push harder in the visible directions.

texts.text: Most brands over-select type. They pick a wordmark font, a headline font, a subheading font, a body font, and a monospace accent, and they think the layered specificity is a strength. It is not. It is a system with five points of failure and no single voice.
